title: The extra bits
objectives: Derive from Jensen's inequality that the KL divergence is never negative, and compute it in bits.

screens.prose: Level 2 so far: the forecaster's code cost 0.123 bits a report above the entropy, and equal chances 0.25 in another town. Step through five models of the weather $p = (0.7, 0.2, 0.1)$.

frames.caption: Too sure of dry: 0.048 extra bits
Equal to the truth: 0 extra bits

screens.question: Can any model's code cost less than the entropy?

options.text: No: the extra cost is least, 0, when the model equals the truth
Yes: a model surer of dry than the truth costs less
options.why: Read the frame: being too sure of dry still costs 0.048 extra bits.

options.text: Yes: equal chances cost least, since they hedge
options.why: Equal chances cost the most here: 0.428 extra bits.

feedback.correct: Every wrong model costs extra; only the truth costs nothing extra.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the extra bits under each model.

explain.text: The extras were 0.428, 0.123, 0.048, 0.033 and 0. None was negative, and 0 came only at $q = p$. This lesson proves that always happens.

screens.prose: The extra cost is the **KL divergence** (Kullback and Leibler): $$D(p \| q) = \sum_i p_i \log_2 \frac{p_i}{q_i} = H(p, q) - H(p).$$ Work it out term by term for the forecaster.
screens.question: Fill in the two missing terms and the total, to 3 places.

feedback.correct: $0.340 - 0.117 - 0.100 = 0.123$ bits, the extra cost found before.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Each term is $p \log_2(p/q)$, and it can be negative.

byKey.sign: You dropped a minus sign. Where $p < q$ the ratio is below 1 and its log is negative.
byKey.abs-sum: You added the sizes of the terms. Two of them are negative.

explain.text: Rain: $0.2 \log_2 \tfrac{0.2}{0.3} = -0.117$. Snow: $0.1 \log_2 \tfrac12 = -0.100$. Single terms can be negative, but the total, 0.123, matches $1.280 - 1.157$.

screens.prose: Now prove $D(p \| q) \ge 0$ for every model $q$. The sums run over outcomes with $p_i > 0$, so each ratio $q_i / p_i$ is defined. Recall Jensen: for a concave $g$, $E[g(X)] \le g(E[X])$.
screens.question: Put the steps in order. Leave out the two that do not belong.

lines.text: $-D(p \| q) = \sum p_i \log_2 \tfrac{q_i}{p_i}$: flipping a fraction flips the sign of its log.
$= E_p\big[\log_2 \tfrac{q(X)}{p(X)}\big]$: a sum weighted by $p_i$ is an expected value under $p$.
$\le \log_2 1 = 0$: those $q_i$ add to at most 1, and $\log_2$ is increasing.

lines.why: $\log_2$ is concave: its chords lie below it, so the average of the logs is at most the log of the average.

lines.text: $= \sum q_i \log_2 \tfrac{q_i}{p_i}$: weigh by the model instead.
lines.why: That is $D(q \| p)$, a different quantity. The weights must stay $p_i$.

hints.text: Begin with $-D(p \| q)$, so you can show it is at most 0.
The middle step is Jensen for the concave $\log_2$.
After Jensen the $p_i$ cancel, leaving $\log_2 \sum q_i$.

feedback.correct: The log is concave, so the average of the logs is at most the log of the average. That is at most $\log_2 1 = 0$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Start from $-D$, write it as an expected value, then use Jensen.

byKey.d1: You used the convex direction. $\log_2$ is concave, so Jensen gives $\le$.
byKey.d2: You swapped the weights to $q$. Keep the weights $p_i$.
byKey.left-out: A step that belongs was left out. The chain has five links and a conclusion.

explain.text: Jensen moves the log outside the average, then the $p_i$ cancel and leave $\sum q_i \le 1$. The hypothesis $p_i > 0$ lets us divide by $p_i$ and read the sum as an average under $p$.

screens.prose: In the proof, step 3 (Jensen) is an equality only when $q_i / p_i$ is the same number $c$ for every outcome with $p_i > 0$. Step 5 is an equality only when those $q_i$ add to exactly 1.
screens.question: So when is $D(p \| q) = 0$?

options.why: Equal chances gave 0.428 extra bits for this weather. Equality needs $q_i = c\,p_i$ with $c = 1$.
Step 5 also needs the $q_i$ to add to 1, which forces $c = 1$.

options.text: Never: the extra cost is always positive

hints.text: Step 5 needs that sum to be 1, so $c = 1$.

feedback.correct: Both steps are equalities only when $q_i = p_i$ for every outcome.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Combine the two conditions.

explain.text: Step 3 needs $q_i = c\,p_i$. Adding over outcomes, step 5 needs $c \sum p_i = c = 1$. So $q = p$, and any other model costs extra.

screens.prose: Take a bent coin $a = (0.9, 0.1)$ and a fair coin $b = (0.5, 0.5)$. Coding tosses of $a$ with a code built for $b$ costs $D(a \| b)$ extra bits a toss.
screens.question: What is $D(a \| b)$, in bits? Give a decimal to 3 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out $\sum a_i \log_2(a_i / b_i)$.

byKey.entropy: That is $H(a)$. The KL is $H(a, b) - H(a) = 1 - 0.469$.

explain.text: $D(a \| b) = H(a, b) - H(a) = 1 - 0.469 = 0.531$ bits: every toss costs 1 bit with the fair code, against 0.469 with the right one.

screens.prose: Now the other way round: tosses come from the fair coin $b$, coded for the bent coin $a$.
screens.question: What is $D(b \| a)$, in bits? Give a decimal to 3 places.

hints.text: Take half of each and add.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Weigh by $b$ now: $\sum b_i \log_2(b_i / a_i)$.

byKey.same: You kept the old order. KL depends on which distribution is the truth.

explain.text: $D(b \| a) = H(b, a) - H(b) = 1.737 - 1 = 0.737$ bits. The bent code gives tails 3.32 bits, and fair tails come half the time. KL is not symmetric, so it is not a distance.

screens.prose: Machine learning code usually works in nats, with $\ln$. A KL divergence in nats is the one in bits times $\ln 2$.
screens.question: What is $D(a \| b)$ in nats? Give a decimal to 3 places.

byKey.divided: You divided by $\ln 2$. A nat is larger than a bit, so there are fewer nats.
byKey.bits: That is the figure in bits.

screens.prose: A colleague checks the old pair: $p = (\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac18)$ against equal chances $u$. She finds $D(p \| u) = 0.25$ and $D(u \| p) = 0.25$.
screens.question: What should she conclude?

options.text: Nothing general: this pair matches by chance
KL is symmetric, so the order of $p$ and $q$ never matters
options.why: One example cannot show a rule. The coins $a$ and $b$ gave 0.531 one way and 0.737 the other.

options.text: KL is a true distance between the two distributions
options.why: A distance is symmetric, and KL is not: the coins break it.

hints.text: Is there a pair where the orders differ?

feedback.correct: One matching pair is a coincidence, not a rule.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Recall the two coins.

byKey.symmetric: You generalised from one pair. The coins break the rule at once.
byKey.distance: You read KL as a distance. It is not symmetric.

explain.text: $D(p \| u) = 2 - 1.75$ and $D(u \| p) = 2.25 - 2$, both 0.25 by chance. For the coins the two orders give 0.531 and 0.737.

screens.prose: Let $p = (0.5, 0.5, 0)$ and $q = (0.25, 0.25, 0.5)$. The model $q$ allows a third outcome that $p$ rules out.
screens.question: Which is true?

options.text: $D(p \| q) = 1$ bit, and $D(q \| p)$ is infinite
Both are infinite, since a zero appears
options.why: $D(p \| q)$ skips the third term, where $p = 0$. Each other term is $0.5 \log_2 2$.
$D(q \| p)$ has the term $0.5 \log_2(0.5 / 0)$, which has no bound.

options.text: $D(p \| q)$ is infinite and $D(q \| p) = 1$ bit
options.why: You put the zero in the wrong place. Trouble comes when the second distribution is 0 where the first is not.

hints.text: The third weight is $p_3 = 0$, so that term goes.
In $D(q \| p)$ the third term divides by $p_3 = 0$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Check which distribution has the zero, and whether it is the weight or the divisor.

byKey.reversed: You put the zero on the wrong side. A zero weight is harmless; a zero divisor is not.

explain.text: $D(p \| q) = 0.5 \log_2 2 + 0.5 \log_2 2 + 0 = 1$ bit. $D(q \| p)$ weighs $\log_2(0.5 / 0)$ by 0.5: a code built for $p$ has no word for the third outcome.

explain.text:
The same two checks as the cross-entropy, in the same order, with infinity in place of the error.

```python

    continue
if qi == 0:
    return math.inf
total += pi * math.log2(pi / qi)
```

screens.prose: A model gives next-day return buckets (big fall, fall, rise, big rise) chances 0.1, 0.4, 0.4, 0.1. Over two years the realised shares were 0.15, 0.35, 0.35, 0.15.
screens.question: What is $D(\text{realised} \| \text{model})$, in bits per day? Give a decimal to 3 places.

hints.text: Each pair appears twice: work out $2(0.15 \times 0.585 + 0.35 \times (-0.193))$.

feedback.correct: About 0.041 bits a day: the price of the model's thin tails.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Weigh $\log_2(\text{realised}/\text{model})$ by the realised shares.

byKey.reversed: You weighed by the model. The days came from the realised shares.

explain.text: $2(0.15 \times 0.585 + 0.35 \times (-0.193)) \approx 0.041$ bits a day, about 10 bits over 250 days. KL prices the model's error in the units of a code.

ideas: The KL divergence $D(p \| q) = \sum p_i \log_2(p_i/q_i) = H(p, q) - H(p)$ is the extra cost of coding $p$ with a code built for $q$.
By Jensen, since $\log$ is concave and the sum runs over $p_i > 0$: $D(p \| q) \ge 0$, with equality only when $q = p$.
KL is not symmetric: $D(a \| b) = 0.531$ but $D(b \| a) = 0.737$ bits. It is infinite when $q_i = 0 < p_i$.
summary.trap: Reading KL as symmetric from one pair: $(\tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \tfrac18)$ against equal chances gives 0.25 both ways by coincidence.

feedback.generic: Not quite. KL is the cross-entropy minus the entropy.

byKey.cross: That is the whole cost. Subtract $H(p) = 1$.

quiz.prose: A student reports $D(p \| q) = -0.05$ bits for two distributions that each add to 1.
quiz.question: What follows?

options.text: There is a mistake: KL is never negative
The model beats the truth by 0.05 bits
options.why: No model codes the truth more cheaply than the truth itself.

options.text: They are fine: KL is negative when $q$ is sharper
options.why: Single terms can be negative, but the sum cannot.

feedback.correct: By Jensen, $D(p \| q) \ge 0$ whenever both add to 1.

explain.text: The proof gave $-D \le \log_2 \sum q_i \le 0$. A negative total means an arithmetic slip, or a $q$ that adds to more than 1.
